headline: The $67 million behind six Senate races, and what it bought
dek: A crypto super PAC was the biggest outside spender in The Watch's federal data, and most of its money went into an Alabama primary. The filings so far show only part of what the national players spent.
summary: The side with more outside money won all five decided Senate races in our data, but the filings undercount several big spenders.

paras.text: The Federal Election Commission figures The Watch pulled on Nov. 7 show $67.0 million in independent expenditures in six U.S. Senate races. Independent expenditures are ads and other spending by groups that may not coordinate with candidates. No House race appears in the pull, and no committee in it itemized a direct payment to Meta or Google. So this is a partial map. For scale, ad spending hit a record $11.87 billion, according to AdImpact. Google's own transparency report shows $1.4 billion in political ads on its platforms since January 2025.
The map still says something. The biggest single spender was a crypto-industry super PAC, and most of its money went into a Republican primary.
Where the money came from

Defend American Jobs spent $12.2 million, all of it in Alabama. That is nearly a fifth of the total. It is a Republican affiliate of crypto super PAC Fairshake. In the second half of 2025, Fairshake's three biggest donors gave $74 million: Ripple and Coinbase each donating $25 million and Andreessen Horowitz contributing $24 million. An FEC analysis by FinTech Weekly counted Coinbase as the single largest contributor to Fairshake in the current cycle with a combined total of $52,469,213.87.

On the Democratic side, much of the money traces back to Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. The Georgia Way raised $8,500,095.00 between June and mid-October. Votelog, a site that compiles FEC filings, lists Senate Majority PAC as its donor for $8,500,000. Lower Costs Now got nearly all of its money from two committees: SMP, which contributed $30 million, and FF PAC, which gave $20 million.

On the Republican side, the Alabama Freedom Fund is bankrolled by Club for Growth Action. In Arkansas, the Democrat-Gazette reported that America One received $450,000 from America One Policies, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, and a combined $250,000 from members of the Stephens family. A 501(c)(4) is a nonprofit that does not have to name its donors. The biggest Republican Senate super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, has a similar arrangement: it is closely affiliated with One Nation, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit organization that is not legally required to publicly disclose its donors. A newer industry also gave. Reuters reported that prediction-market operators Kalshi and Polymarket gave at least $5 million combined to Republican and Democratic political groups.
Where it went

Alabama drew the most outside money: $22.5 million, with $19.4 million on the Republican side. One thing about how The Watch's data counts money matters here. Spending against a Republican goes in the Democratic column, even when another Republican paid for it. So almost all of Alabama's $3.1 million "for Democrats" is Republicans attacking Republicans. Roll Call reported that the Alabama Freedom Fund spent $2.5 million to boost his campaign and to oppose Marshall. Meanwhile, American Values First has been boosting Marshall and opposing Hudson. Votelog counts only $387,557 of independent expenditures disseminated after the June 16, 2026 primary runoffs.

Georgia drew $20.9 million, $19.3 million of it on the Democratic side. That includes $4.2 million from Hardworking Americans Inc., Kemp's super PAC, the committee of Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, which was active in the Republican primary. Our data shows just $1.6 million helping Republicans in Georgia. Other counts are higher: Votelog lists the Senate Leadership Fund at $11,511,399, all opposing Ossoff. The super PAC had committed to spending $44 million in Georgia. AdImpact later said it had recently canceled $7.6 million in ad reservations in Georgia.

In Alaska, our data shows Democrats ahead, $12.5 million to $5.4 million. Local reporting found the opposite. The Anchorage Daily News reported that Sen. Dan Sullivan's allies had spent roughly $20 million on ads attacking Peltola and supporting the incumbent since mid-July, against about $15.4 million from Mary Peltola's backers. According to AdImpact, Republicans have reserved $45 million in Alaska advertising from Aug. 1 through Election Day, compared with Democrats' $32 million.
In Arkansas, America One directed $4.5 million on media opposing Shoffner, the Democrat Hallie Shoffner. The Colorado and Florida races drew less than $1 million each.
Where the ads ran

The data block shows zero direct payments to Meta or Google. That does not mean no money reached them. Committees usually pay media-buying firms, which then buy the airtime and the digital ads, so direct platform payments are only a floor. For example, the Senate Leadership Fund's filings show media placement paid to Cavalry LLC, and media production paid to SLMG LLC. AB PAC spent on billboard advertising paid to AdQuick, Lamar Companies and Target Platform.

Google's own report fills in some of the gap. The SLF PAC spent $34.6 million on Google's platforms, mostly in Ohio and Michigan. WinSenate spent $33.5 million, Jon Ossoff's campaign $23.0 million, and two accounts registered as One Nation a combined $26.3 million. The biggest political advertiser on Google was Kalshi, at $84.2 million. Spending peaked in the week of Oct. 25, at $171.8 million.

Television still got the most money. Defend American Jobs said its Alabama ad will air on TV, streaming and Fox News Channel. The Alabama Freedom Fund's buy covered TV, streaming and radio in the Birmingham and Huntsville media markets. In the third quarter, broadcast television accounted for 51% of the $3 billion in political advertising that aired.
What the ads said

The crypto PAC's ads were mostly about President Donald Trump: the first one highlighting President Donald Trump's endorsement of Moore. The group also promised he would help make America the crypto capital. The Club for Growth's ad called Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall someone who had spent most of his life as a "soft-on-crime Democrat." Marshall changed his party affiliation from Democrat to Republican in 2011.

In Alaska, a North Star ad criticizes Sullivan for accepting hundreds of thousands of dollars from commercial trawling companies, linking the industry to declines in salmon runs. On the other side, Last Frontier PAC turned a New York Times report on Peltola's treatment of her staff into a grainy black-and-white attack ad. FactCheck.org found that ads from Sullivan and the PAC misleadingly claim that Peltola opposed military pay raises. In the final week, 59 PAC, an SLF affiliate group in Alaska, and Last Frontier PAC paid for ads tying Peltola to a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Peltola's campaign has continued to deny involvement.
In Arkansas, America One's ads went after Shoffner over her comments on migrant workers and opposition toward the Trump administration's controversial immigration enforcement agenda.
Whether it worked
In our data, the side with more outside money won all five decided races. Look closer and the record is mixed.

- **Alabama:** Most of the money was spent before the nomination. The crypto PAC's candidate, Barry Moore, won the runoff over Jared Hudson, who lost the Republican primary runoff to Moore. He then beat Democrat Everett Wess by 9.4 points in the general election, which drew little outside money.
- **Georgia:** Ossoff won by 18 points. But Republicans' main group pulled back, and his campaign had its own money: $2.1 million in cash on hand as of June 30 for Collins, against $42.6 million for Ossoff.
- **Arkansas:** Tom Cotton won by 11.9 points. That is not close to Trump's electoral performance in Arkansas two years ago, when he carried the state by nearly 31 points.
- **Alaska:** The race has not been called. Our results show Sullivan up 2.0 points. Alaska Public Media reported that by Wednesday Peltola led Sullivan by 637 votes, and The Washington Post reported she held a narrow lead going into the weekend. If Sullivan holds on, the side with less money in our data wins. By the press's counts, it would be the side that spent more.
Nationally, AdImpact found Republicans spending approximately $5.18 billion this election cycle, compared with $4.77 billion for Democrats.
